title: Number Sentences: Missing Numbers and Equations
seo_title: Grade 5 Number Sentences Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
standard_text: Write number sentences to describe problem situations; solve and complete number sentences by inspection and by trial and improvement; check solutions by substitution.
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 5 number sentences worksheets: missing numbers, letters for unknowns, checking by substitution and writing number sentences. 100 questions with memos.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • A number sentence uses = to show that both sides have the same value: 45 + ☐ = 120.
  • Use the inverse operation to find the missing number: ☐ = 120 − 45 = 75.
  • A letter can stand for the missing number: 8 × n = 96, so n = 12.
  • Check by putting the number back into the sentence (substitution).

Examples

Example

☐ ÷ 6 = 34

inverse: 34 × 6

Answer: ☐ = 204

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
The same operationUse the inverse.
= means the answer= means the same value on both sides.
Wrong operationRead what the story does.

items.e: Use the inverse. Subtraction undoes addition: n = 45 − 18 = 27. Check: 27 + 18 = 45. Not 63: that adds, the same operation, instead of subtracting. Not 33: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.
n is the number you start with. Undo − 12 by adding: n = 30 + 12 = 42. Check: 42 − 12 = 30. Not 18: that subtracts, the same operation, instead of adding.

Use the inverse. Subtraction undoes addition: n = 4 000 − 1 250 = 2 750. Check: 1 250 + 2 750 = 4 000. Not 5 250: that adds, the same operation, instead of subtracting. Not 3 250: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

600 take away what leaves 275? m = 600 − 275 = 325. Check: 600 − 325 = 275. Not 875: that adds the two numbers. Not 475: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

t is the number you start with. Undo − 2 750 by adding: t = 6 500 + 2 750 = 9 250. Check: 9 250 − 2 750 = 6 500. Not 3 750: that subtracts, the same operation, instead of adding. Not 8 250: that forgets to carry.

n is the number you start with. Undo − 25 000 by adding: n = 75 000 + 25 000 = 100 000. Check: 100 000 − 25 000 = 75 000. Not 50 000: that subtracts, the same operation, instead of adding. Not 90 000: that forgets to carry.
The = sign can come first. n + 35 = 90, so n = 90 − 35 = 55. Check: 55 + 35 = 90. Not 125: that adds. Not 65: that takes the smaller digit from the larger.
The = sign can come first. 925 − w = 350, so w = 925 − 350 = 575. Check: 925 − 575 = 350. Not 1 275: that adds the two numbers. Not 635: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

items.q: 275 + n = 650. What is n?
items.e: Use the inverse. Subtraction undoes addition: n = 650 − 275 = 375. Check: 275 + 375 = 650. Not 925: that adds, the same operation, instead of subtracting. Not 425: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

items.q: n − 1 400 = 2 600. What is n?
items.e: n is the number you start with. Undo − 1 400 by adding: n = 2 600 + 1 400 = 4 000. Check: 4 000 − 1 400 = 2 600. Not 1 200: that subtracts, the same operation, instead of adding. Not 3 000: that forgets to carry.

items.q: Aisha solves n + 27 = 63 and gets n = 90. What did she do wrong?
items.e: 90 + 27 is 117, not 63. She used the same operation, addition, instead of the inverse. Undo + 27 by subtracting: n = 63 − 27 = 36. Check: 36 + 27 = 63.

items.q: Precious solves n + 27 = 63 and gets n = 90. What did she do wrong?
items.e: 90 + 27 is 117, not 63. She used the same operation, addition, instead of the inverse. Undo + 27 by subtracting: n = 63 − 27 = 36. Check: 36 + 27 = 63.

items.e: 90 + 27 is 117, not 63. She used the same operation, addition, instead of the inverse. Undo + 27 by subtracting: n = 63 − 27 = 36. Check: 36 + 27 = 63.
6n means 6 × n. Division undoes multiplication: n = 42 ÷ 6 = 7. Check: 6 × 7 = 42. Not 36: that reads 6n as 6 + n. Not 252: that multiplies instead of dividing.
4n means 4 × n. Division undoes multiplication: n = 28 ÷ 4 = 7. Check: 4 × 7 = 28. Not 24: that reads 4n as 4 + n. Not 112: that multiplies instead of dividing.
8k means 8 × k. Division undoes multiplication: k = 96 ÷ 8 = 12. Check: 8 × 12 = 96. Not 88: that reads 8k as 8 + k. Not 768: that multiplies instead of dividing.
7y means 7 × y. Division undoes multiplication: y = 56 ÷ 7 = 8. Check: 7 × 8 = 56. Not 49: that reads 7y as 7 + y. Not 392: that multiplies instead of dividing.
12n means 12 × n. Division undoes multiplication: n = 108 ÷ 12 = 9. Check: 12 × 9 = 108. Not 96: that reads 12n as 12 + n. Not 1 296: that multiplies instead of dividing.
5m means 5 × m. Division undoes multiplication: m = 300 ÷ 5 = 60. Check: 5 × 60 = 300. Think 30 tens ÷ 5 = 6 tens. Not 6: that drops the zero. Not 295: that subtracts. Not 1 500: that multiplies.

20t means 20 × t. Division undoes multiplication: t = 160 ÷ 20 = 8. Check: 20 × 8 = 160. Think 16 tens ÷ 2 tens = 8. Not 140: that subtracts. Not 3 200: that multiplies. Not 80: that divides by 2 instead of 20.
Division undoes multiplication: n = 44 ÷ 4 = 11. Check: 11 × 4 = 44. Not 40: that subtracts. Not 176: that multiplies instead of dividing.
n is the number you start with. Multiplication undoes division: n = 9 × 4 = 36. Check: 36 ÷ 4 = 9. Not 13: that adds. Not 5: that subtracts. Not 32: that is 8 × 4.
n is the number you start with. Multiplication undoes division: n = 8 × 6 = 48. Check: 48 ÷ 6 = 8. Not 14: that adds. Not 2: that subtracts. Not 42: that is 7 × 6.
a is the number you start with. Multiplication undoes division: a = 15 × 3 = 45. Check: 45 ÷ 3 = 15. Not 5: that divides again, the same operation, instead of multiplying. Not 18: that adds.
p is the number you start with. Multiplication undoes division: p = 25 × 10 = 250. Check: 250 ÷ 10 = 25. Not 35: that adds. Not 15: that subtracts. Not 2 500: that writes one zero too many.

Ask: 48 divided by what gives 6? w = 48 ÷ 6 = 8. Check: 48 ÷ 8 = 6. Not 288: that multiplies. Not 42: that subtracts.
The = sign can come first. 6n = 54, so n = 54 ÷ 6 = 9. Check: 6 × 9 = 54. Not 48: that reads 6n as 6 + n. Not 324: that multiplies.
The = sign can come first. n ÷ 8 = 7, so n = 7 × 8 = 56. Check: 56 ÷ 8 = 7. Not 15: that adds. Not 1: that subtracts. Not 48: that is 6 × 8.

items.q: The pans balance. What is n?
items.e: 3n = 33, so n = 33 ÷ 3 = 11. Check: 3 × 11 = 33. Not 30: that reads 3n as 3 + n. Not 99: that multiplies.

items.q: The bar shows 5 equal parts of n that make 65. 5n = 65. What is n?
items.e: 5 equal parts make 65, so n = 65 ÷ 5 = 13. Check: 5 × 13 = 65. Not 60: that subtracts. Not 325: that multiplies.

items.q: The bar shows n cut into 4 equal parts of 13. n ÷ 4 = 13. What is n?
items.e: n is the whole. Put the 4 parts together: n = 13 × 4 = 52. Check: 52 ÷ 4 = 13. Not 17: that adds. Not 9: that subtracts. Not 48: that is 12 × 4.

items.q: Zinhle solves 6n = 48 and gets n = 42. What did she do wrong?
items.e: 48 − 6 = 42, so Zinhle solved 6 + n = 48. But 6n means 6 × n. n = 48 ÷ 6 = 8. Check: 6 × 8 = 48.

Undo + 17 by subtracting 17 from both sides: n = 45 − 17 = 28. Check: 28 + 17 = 45. Wrong answers: 62 comes from adding 17 instead of subtracting it; 32 comes from taking 5 − 7 as 7 − 5; 38 comes from regrouping but not taking 1 away from the tens.

Undo − 23 by adding 23 to both sides: n = 58 + 23 = 81. Check: 81 − 23 = 58. Wrong answers: 35 comes from subtracting instead of adding; 71 comes from forgetting to carry the 1 ten; 711 comes from writing 8 + 3 = 11 in the ones place without regrouping.

6n means 6 × n. Undo × 6 by dividing both sides by 6: n = 54 ÷ 6 = 9. Check: 6 × 9 = 54. Wrong answers: 48 comes from subtracting 6 instead of dividing; 324 comes from multiplying by 6 instead of dividing; 60 comes from adding 6.

Undo ÷ 4 by multiplying both sides by 4: n = 9 × 4 = 36. Check: 36 ÷ 4 = 9. Wrong answers: 13 comes from adding 4 instead of multiplying; 5 comes from subtracting 4; 32 comes from using 4 × 8 instead of 4 × 9.
Divide both sides by 7: n = 63 ÷ 7 = 9. Check: 7 × 9 = 63. Wrong answers: 56 comes from subtracting 7 instead of dividing; 70 comes from adding 7; 8 comes from a fact slip (7 × 8 = 56, not 63).
Multiply both sides by 5: n = 8 × 5 = 40. Check: 40 ÷ 5 = 8. Wrong answers: 13 comes from adding 5 instead of multiplying; 3 comes from subtracting 5; 45 comes from using 5 × 9.

The letter can be on the right side. Subtract 19 from both sides: 45 − 19 = 26, so n = 26. Check: 26 + 19 = 45. Wrong answers: 64 comes from adding 19 instead of subtracting it; 34 comes from taking 5 − 9 as 9 − 5; 36 comes from regrouping but not taking 1 away from the tens.

30 take away some number is 12. The number taken away is 30 − 12 = 18. Check: 30 − 18 = 12. Wrong answers: 42 comes from adding 30 + 12; 22 comes from taking 2 − 0 instead of regrouping; 8 comes from subtracting 12 from 20 instead of 30.
48 divided by some number is 6. Since 6 × 8 = 48, n = 48 ÷ 6 = 8. Check: 48 ÷ 8 = 6. Wrong answers: 288 comes from multiplying 48 × 6; 42 comes from subtracting 6; 54 comes from adding 6.
Divide both sides by 9: n = 72 ÷ 9 = 8. Check: 9 × 8 = 72. Wrong answers: 63 comes from subtracting 9 instead of dividing; 81 comes from adding 9; 648 comes from multiplying by 9 instead of dividing.

items.q: The pan balance is level. Each block has the same mass, n. What is n?
items.e: The balance shows 2n + 8 = 20. Take 8 off both pans: 2n = 12. 2 equal blocks make 12, so each block is 12 ÷ 2 = 6. Check: 2 × 6 + 8 = 20. Wrong answers: 12 comes from stopping at 2n = 12; 14 comes from adding 8 instead of subtracting it; 2 comes from dividing first: 20 ÷ 2 − 8.

items.q: The pan balance is level. Each block has the same mass, n. What is n?
items.e: The balance shows 3n + 4 = 19. Take 4 off both pans: 3n = 15. 3 equal blocks make 15, so each block is 15 ÷ 3 = 5. Check: 3 × 5 + 4 = 19. Wrong answers: 15 comes from stopping at 3n = 15; 12 comes from subtracting 3 instead of dividing by 3; 45 comes from multiplying 15 by 3 instead of dividing.

Subtract 3 from both sides: 2n = 12. Then divide both sides by 2: n = 12 ÷ 2 = 6. Check: 2 × 6 + 3 = 15. Wrong answers: 12 comes from stopping at 2n = 12; 9 comes from adding 3 instead of subtracting it; 10 comes from subtracting 2 instead of dividing by 2.

Add 2 to both sides: 3n = 27. Then divide both sides by 3: n = 27 ÷ 3 = 9. Check: 3 × 9 − 2 = 25. Wrong answers: 27 comes from stopping at 3n = 27; 24 comes from subtracting 3 instead of dividing by 3; 81 comes from multiplying 27 by 3.

Subtract 5 from both sides: 4n = 36. Then divide both sides by 4: n = 36 ÷ 4 = 9. Check: 4 × 9 + 5 = 41. Wrong answers: 36 comes from stopping at 4n = 36; 32 comes from subtracting 4 instead of dividing by 4; 144 comes from multiplying 36 by 4.

Subtract 10 from both sides: 5n = 50. Then divide both sides by 5: n = 50 ÷ 5 = 10. Check: 5 × 10 + 10 = 60. Wrong answers: 50 comes from stopping at 5n = 50; 14 comes from adding 10 instead of subtracting it; 2 comes from dividing first: 60 ÷ 5 − 10.

Add 6 to both sides: 6n = 36. Then divide both sides by 6: n = 36 ÷ 6 = 6. Check: 6 × 6 − 6 = 30. Wrong answers: 36 comes from stopping at 6n = 36; 4 comes from subtracting 6 instead of adding it; 24 comes from subtracting 6 from 30 and stopping.

items.q: What is the best first step to solve 3n + 5 = 26?
items.e: 3n + 5 means “multiply by 3, then add 5.” Undo in reverse order: first subtract 5 from both sides to get 3n = 21, then divide by 3 to get n = 7.

items.q: What should you do to solve n ÷ 6 = 7?
items.e: The opposite of dividing by 6 is multiplying by 6: n = 7 × 6 = 42. Check: 42 ÷ 6 = 7.

n + n is 2n, so 2n + 9 = 25. Subtract 9: 2n = 16. Divide by 2: n = 8. Check: 8 + 8 + 9 = 25. Wrong answers: 16 comes from stopping at n + n = 16; 17 comes from adding 9 instead of subtracting it; 14 comes from reading n + n as n + 2.
To check, put the value back into the equation. 27 + 18 = 45, so yes. 27 + 18 = 35 forgets to carry the ten. 63 is 45 + 18, the same operation.
Put 18 into the equation: 18 − 12 = 6, not 30. So no. The solution is 30 + 12 = 42. 18 + 12 = 30 and 30 − 12 = 18 are true facts, but they do not put 18 into n − 12 = 30.
6k means 6 × k. 6 × 7 = 42, so yes. 6 + 7 reads 6k as 6 + k. 67 writes the digits side by side. 6 × 7 is 42, not 48.
Put 2 into the equation: 2 ÷ 4 is less than 1, not 8. So no. The solution is 8 × 4 = 32. 8 ÷ 4 = 2 and 2 × 4 = 8 are true facts, but they do not put 2 into n ÷ 4 = 8. 12 adds 8 and 4.

items.q: Yusuf solves n − 15 = 40 and gets n = 25. Check his answer. What is true?
items.e: Put 25 back into n − 15 = 40: 25 − 15 = 10, not 40. So the answer is wrong. Undo − 15 by adding: n = 40 + 15 = 55. 45 − 15 is 30, so 45 is wrong too.
Put 9 into the equation: 72 ÷ 9 = 8, so yes. 576 is 72 × 8. 64 is 72 − 8.
30 000 + 18 000 = 48 000, not 50 000, so no. Close is not enough: both sides must be equal. The solution is 50 000 − 18 000 = 32 000.
Put 6 into each one. 7 × 6 = 42, so 7n = 42. The others give 6 + 9 = 15, 6 − 4 = 2 and 6 ÷ 2 = 3.

items.q: Nomsa solved n + 18 = 50 and got n = 68. Which is the correct way to check her answer?
items.e: To check, put the answer back into the original equation: 68 + 18 = 86, not 50. So 68 is wrong. The right answer is 50 − 18 = 32 (check: 32 + 18 = 50). Doing the same work again, or using the opposite operation, does not test the answer.

items.q: Elna solved n − 16 = 25 and got n = 31. Which is the correct way to check her answer?
c: 31 is greater than 25, so 31 is right
items.e: Put 31 back into the original equation: 31 − 16 = 15, not 25. So 31 is wrong. The right answer is 25 + 16 = 41 (the 1 ten was not carried). Check: 41 − 16 = 25.

items.q: Lerato solved 4n = 36 and got n = 32. Which is the correct way to check her answer?
items.e: 4n means 4 × n. Put 32 back in: 4 × 32 = 128, not 36. So 32 is wrong. The right answer is 36 ÷ 4 = 9 (check: 4 × 9 = 36).

items.q: Which number is the solution of 2n + 7 = 25? Test each choice.
items.e: Test each choice in the equation. 2 × 9 + 7 = 25 ✓; 2 × 18 + 7 = 43; 2 × 16 + 7 = 39; 2 × 8 + 7 = 23.

items.q: Which number is the solution of 5n − 3 = 32? Test each choice.
Which number is the solution of n ÷ 4 + 2 = 9? Test each choice.
items.e: Test each choice in the equation. 28 ÷ 4 + 2 = 9 ✓; 7 ÷ 4 is not a whole number; 44 ÷ 4 + 2 = 13; 34 ÷ 4 is not a whole number.

items.q: Which number is the solution of n + n + n = 27? Test each choice.
Lerato solved n + 18 = 50 and got n = 68. Which is the correct way to check her answer?
items.e: To check, put the answer back into the original equation: 68 + 18 = 86, not 50. So 68 is wrong. The right answer is 50 − 18 = 32 (check: 32 + 18 = 50). Doing the same work again, or using the opposite operation, does not test the answer.

items.q: Ruan solved n − 16 = 25 and got n = 31. Which is the correct way to check his answer?
c: 31 is greater than 25, so 31 is right
items.e: Put 31 back into the original equation: 31 − 16 = 15, not 25. So 31 is wrong. The right answer is 25 + 16 = 41 (the 1 ten was not carried). Check: 41 − 16 = 25.

items.q: Mbali solved 4n = 36 and got n = 32. Which is the correct way to check her answer?
items.e: 4n means 4 × n. Put 32 back in: 4 × 32 = 128, not 36. So 32 is wrong. The right answer is 36 ÷ 4 = 9 (check: 4 × 9 = 36).

items.q: A school orders 6 boxes of pencils with n pencils in each box. There are 144 pencils in all. Which equation matches?
items.e: 6 equal groups of n make 144: 6n = 144. Equal groups mean ×, not +. Then n = 144 ÷ 6 = 24.

items.q: A class shares a pack of s stickers equally among 4 groups. Each group gets 18 stickers. Which equation matches?
items.e: Start with s, share into 4 groups and get 18 in each: s ÷ 4 = 18. Then s = 18 × 4 = 72.

items.q: “Eight times a number is 96.” Which equation matches?
items.e: “Eight times a number” is 8 × n, written 8n: 8n = 96. Then n = 96 ÷ 8 = 12.

items.q: Volunteers count salmon swimming up a creek. They count 1 450 salmon in the first week. After two weeks the total is 4 000. How many did they count in the second week?
items.e: Equation: 1 450 + n = 4 000. n = 4 000 − 1 450 = 2 550 salmon. Check: 1 450 + 2 550 = 4 000. Not 5 450: that adds. Not 3 450: that takes the smaller digit from the larger in each column.

items.q: Ravi plants cedar seedlings in 8 equal rows. There are 15 seedlings in each row. How many seedlings did he plant?
items.e: Equation: n ÷ 8 = 15. Undo ÷ 8 by multiplying: n = 15 × 8 = 120 seedlings. Check: 120 ÷ 8 = 15. Not 23: that adds. Not 7: that subtracts. Not 135: that is 15 × 9.

items.q: Juice boxes come in packs of 12. The school needs 180 juice boxes for Sports Day. How many packs does it need?
items.e: Equation: 12p = 180. p = 180 ÷ 12 = 15 packs. Check: 12 × 15 = 180. Not 168: that subtracts. Not 2 160: that multiplies.

items.q: A school wants to collect 15 000 cans for the food bank. So far it has 8 750 cans. How many more cans does it need?
items.e: Equation: 8 750 + c = 15 000. c = 15 000 − 8 750 = 6 250 cans. Check: 8 750 + 6 250 = 15 000. Not 23 750: that adds. Not 13 750: that takes the smaller digit from the larger.

items.q: A school library packs 252 books into 9 boxes with the same number in each box. How many books go in each box?
items.e: Equation: 9b = 252. b = 252 ÷ 9 = 28 books. Check: 9 × 28 = 252. Not 243: that reads 9b as 9 + b. Not 2 268: that multiplies.

items.q: Ethan plants cedar seedlings in 8 equal rows. There are 15 seedlings in each row. How many seedlings did he plant?
items.e: Equation: n ÷ 8 = 15. Undo ÷ 8 by multiplying: n = 15 × 8 = 120 seedlings. Check: 120 ÷ 8 = 15. Not 23: that adds. Not 7: that subtracts. Not 135: that is 15 × 9.

items.q: Sarah plants cedar seedlings in 8 equal rows. There are 15 seedlings in each row. How many seedlings did she plant?
items.e: Equation: n ÷ 8 = 15. Undo ÷ 8 by multiplying: n = 15 × 8 = 120 seedlings. Check: 120 ÷ 8 = 15. Not 23: that adds. Not 7: that subtracts. Not 135: that is 15 × 9.

items.q: Dumisani puts 72 sausages onto 9 trays for the fundraiser, with the same number on each tray. Which number sentence shows how many sausages go on each tray?
items.e: 72 sausages are shared equally into 9 groups, so divide: 72 ÷ 9 = ? (? = 8). 9 ÷ 72 is the wrong way round: the total comes first.

items.q: Megan buys 6 packets of stickers. Each packet has the same number of stickers. She gets 54 stickers altogether. How many stickers are in each packet?
items.e: Number sentence: 6 × ? = 54. Use the inverse: ? = 54 ÷ 6 = 9. Check: 6 × 9 = 54. Not 48: that subtracts 6 from 54.

items.q: A teacher shares some pencils equally among 6 tables. Each table gets 9 pencils. Which number sentence matches the story?
items.e: You do not know how many pencils there are in total, so the total is ?: ? ÷ 6 = 9. Then ? = 9 × 6 = 54 pencils.

items.q: Eggs come in boxes of 12. The school tuck shop uses 96 eggs in a week. How many boxes of eggs is that?
items.e: Number sentence: ? × 12 = 96. Use the inverse: ? = 96 ÷ 12 = 8 boxes. Check: 8 × 12 = 96. Not 1 152: that multiplies instead of dividing.

items.q: Lwazi shares 84 lion stickers equally among some friends. Each friend gets 7 stickers. How many friends are there?
items.e: Number sentence: 84 ÷ ? = 7. ? = 84 ÷ 7 = 12 friends. Check: 84 ÷ 12 = 7. Not 77: that subtracts 7 from 84.

items.q: Zinhle runs the same distance every day for 5 days to train for the cross-country. She runs 35 km in total. Which number sentence shows how far she runs each day?
items.e: Each day is the same distance, ?, and 5 days make 35 km: 5 × ? = 35. Then ? = 35 ÷ 5 = 7 km. ? ÷ 5 = 35 would mean 35 km each day.

items.q: At the athletics day, the Grade 5 learners are split into 8 teams of 7. How many Grade 5 learners are there?
items.e: Number sentence: ? ÷ 8 = 7. Use the inverse: ? = 7 × 8 = 56 learners. Check: 56 ÷ 8 = 7. Not 15: that adds 8 and 7.

items.q: Aisha’s classroom has 4 rows of 7 desks. The class moves the same desks into 2 long rows of equal length. Which number sentence matches?
items.e: Both ways use the same number of desks, so the two sides are equal: 4 × 7 = 2 × ?. Then 28 = 2 × ?, so ? = 14 desks in each long row.

items.q: At the swimming gala, 120 learners swim in heats of 8. How many heats are there?
items.e: Number sentence: 120 ÷ 8 = ?. 120 = 80 + 40, so 120 ÷ 8 = 10 + 5 = 15 heats. Check: 15 × 8 = 120. Not 112: that subtracts 8 from 120.

items.q: Siyabonga works out that 84 ÷ 7 = 12. Which number sentence can he use to check his answer?
items.e: Check a division with the inverse, multiplication: 12 × 7 = 84, so 12 × 7 = 84 shows 84 ÷ 7 = 12 is right. 84 × 7 = 588 is true, but it does not check the division.
